sittings.bodyEn: These slips are expected, because lifestyle design means resisting impulses from the plan that stores life until retirement. The first mistake is losing sight of your dreams and falling into work for work's sake. The repair is to reread the opening of the book and the next chapter whenever the slide starts. Everyone hits this one. The people who stay stuck are the ones who stop noticing. Treat the return as the skill, and treat a perfect streak as unnecessary.

terms.hook: Busyness that has lost the dream it was supposed to fund.

sittings.bodyEn: The second mistake is micromanaging and emailing to fill time. Set the responsibilities, the problem scenarios, the rules, and the limits of what other people may decide. Then stop. Extra messages sent so the hour feels full are the same mistake in another costume. The sanity at stake belongs to everyone you hired so you could leave. A rule you keep editing is a rule you do not yet trust. Write the boundary once, and let a quiet afternoon stay quiet.

The third mistake is handling problems your outsourcers or coworkers can handle. If the task sits inside their role, your hands on it teach them to wait. The automation chapters already gave them a lane. Stepping back into that lane rebuilds the tollbooth you removed. Leave the problem with the person who has the rule for it. Your involvement is for the case their authority does not cover. Doing their job feels helpful and restores the old week.

The fourth mistake is a repeated rescue on one issue, or help with something that is not a crisis. Give if-then rules for everything short of the largest decisions, and give written permission to act inside those rules. State in writing that you will not answer requests the rules already cover. In the author's setup, specialists could fix anything that cost less than four hundred dollars. Review the effect on profit each month or each quarter, and add rules that capture their good inventions. A second rescue is a missing rule, so write the rule instead of repeating the rescue.

terms.hook: A written instruction that lets someone solve a covered problem without asking you again.

sittings.bodyEn: The fifth mistake is chasing customers, especially unqualified or international prospects, after the cash flow already funds your nonfinancial pursuits. More buyers are a goal from the older plan. The pursuits that are not about money are the ones this income was built to support. A prospect who costs a week of exceptions is a step backward once the baseline is met. International orders were already flagged as a heavy way to grow. Spend the surplus on the project the money was for. The chase becomes optional the moment the funding exists.

The sixth mistake is answering email that will not produce a sale, or that a help page or an automatic reply could handle. Those messages feel like work because they arrive addressed to you. Route them to the page or the person who already has the answer. An automatic note that points people to the right place is the model in this chapter. Your inbox is a poor storage system for a standing policy. If a reply cannot change revenue or a real exception, it waits for the batch or it does not get written. Keep your hours for decisions that are actually yours.

The seventh mistake is working where you live, sleep, or are supposed to relax. Designate one space for work and use it only for work, or the day never ends. A mixed room teaches your body that rest is interrupted labor. If the home cannot hold that split, use a shared work space on occasion so the couch stays a couch. The escape fails if every room is an office. Recovery needs a location that has never held the inbox. Draw the boundary in furniture, not only in intention.

The eighth mistake is skipping a thorough eighty-twenty review every two to four weeks, both in the business and in the rest of life. The few activities that produce most of the result drift if you do not look. Personal commitments deserve the same pass, because a freed calendar fills with worthy-sounding obligations. Put the review on a repeating date. Cut or delegate the long tail again, even if you cut it last month. The analysis is maintenance, in the same family as the reports from the absence chapter. A system you never remeasure slides back toward the old week.

terms.hook: A cut, every two to four weeks, that keeps only the few activities producing most of the result.

sittings.bodyEn: The ninth mistake is chasing endless perfection, in personal life or in the work, when great or good enough would do. It often functions as work for work's sake in a cleaner costume. The chapter's language picture is that about ninety-five percent accuracy can take six months of focused effort, while about ninety-eight percent can take twenty to thirty years. Be great at a few things and good enough at the rest. Keep perfection as a direction. Recognize it as a destination you do not arrive at. Ship the version that meets the standard you wrote down.

The tenth mistake is inflating minutiae and small problems so that work feels justified. A minor snag, examined long enough, can impersonate a crisis. The tell is a response larger than the consequence. Write the actual cost of the issue in time or money before you clear the day for it. If the cost is small, leave it inside the rule you already gave someone else. Proportion is a decision you make on paper. Busyness borrowed from a trivial problem is still busyness.

The eleventh mistake is making a non-urgent issue urgent in order to justify work. Ask whether a delay of a week would change anything real. If it would not, the deadline is a costume. The chapter points attention toward life outside the accounts, and it admits that the open space is frightening at first. If meaning is missing, creating it is your job, through the dreams you named or through work that gives purpose, and ideally through both. Urgency is a poor substitute for that creation. Let a non-urgent item stay non-urgent.

The twelfth mistake is treating a single offer, role, or effort as your entire life. The work in front of you is only a bridge into whatever you do next. A rut is something you can leave. Doubt is a signal to take some action. When you are overwhelmed, stop and run the eighty-twenty cut on the business, on personal activities, and on relationships. The length of a life is a reason to keep moving, and also a reason to refuse despair. One muse was a tool, not a final identity.

The thirteenth mistake is ignoring the social rewards of life. Build a circle of positive people whose days have nothing to do with your work. You can create a muse alone if that is the practical path. Living your life alone is a separate choice, and the chapter argues against it. Friendship and love multiply enjoyment that a solo success only starts. Schedule those people with the same seriousness you once gave the office. The point of the freed time is a life that contains other lives.

The thirteen mistakes are ways the old plan refills a freed calendar. They include work for its own sake, managing and emailing to feel busy, doing other people's problems, rescuing the same issue twice, chasing buyers you no longer need, and answering mail that cannot sell. They also include working where you rest, skipping the regular cut, chasing perfection, inflating small problems, inventing urgency, treating one project as your whole life, and dropping the people outside your work. The repair is a rule, a review, or a return to the life you named. A perfect streak is not required. Recall what replaces another rescue on a problem the rules already cover.
sittings.prompt: What should happen the second time a covered problem appears?
choices: Add or point to the written rule, and stop answering that class of request
Handle it yourself so the standard stays high
Email everyone so you stay visible
Start another product so the week feels full
